title: Photoperiod, Autoflower and Seasonal Risk Windows

content.overview: Outdoor cultivar strategy should fit the local season. Photoperiod cultivars respond to changing daylength; autoflowering types have different developmental timing. Neither category removes heat, frost, rain, pest or smoke risk.

vocabulary.definition: A cultivar whose reproductive development is strongly influenced by daylength/night length.
Cannabis type with flowering timing less dependent on photoperiod than conventional photoperiod cultivars.
Seasonal period in which a hazard such as frost, rain or heat overlaps a vulnerable crop stage.

sections.title: Daylength interacts with genotype
sections.body: Photoperiodic flowering behavior varies genetically; latitude and artificial light exposure can influence timing.

sections.title: Shorter calendar does not mean no weather risk
sections.body: Autoflowering plants may shift harvest timing but still require a season with appropriate establishment and flowering conditions.

sections.title: Plan harvest exposure backward
sections.body: Compare expected flowering/harvest window with local rain, frost, heat and smoke history rather than selecting only by advertised days-to-finish.

workedExamples: A fast cultivar may avoid autumn rain but face midsummer heat if planted too early for the local climate.
Security lighting near a photoperiod crop can become an unintended night-interruption variable.
commonMistakes: Treating advertised days as exact outdoors.
Ignoring local daylength and artificial-night-light exposure.
content.practicalApplication: Build a seasonal calendar with local daylength, frost/heat/rain history and plausible cultivar development ranges, then identify vulnerable overlap windows.
content.summary: Outdoor cultivar choice is risk-timing design, not simply a choice between auto and photo labels.
